topic: Rendering pipeline: measure, layout, draw & RenderThread

questions.question: In what order does a View hierarchy traversal run its passes?
options: Layout, then measure, then draw
Draw, then measure, then layout
Measure and draw together, then layout
Measure, then layout, then draw
questions.explanation: Parents first measure children to learn their desired sizes, then lay them out at final positions, and only then is the tree drawn. Layout needs measured sizes, and drawing needs final positions, so the order cannot change.

questions.question: Calling `invalidate()` on a View schedules a new measure and layout pass for it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `invalidate()` only marks the view as needing to be redrawn. `requestLayout()` is what schedules measure and layout, and you need it when a change affects size or position, like new text in a wrap_content view.

questions.question: With 'Debug GPU overdraw' turned on, large areas of a screen are red. What does that tell you?
options: Those pixels are drawn four or more times per frame, often from stacked opaque backgrounds
Those areas are being redrawn on every frame
Those views took longer than 16 ms to draw
Those views failed to render on the GPU and fell back to software
questions.explanation: The overdraw colors count how many times a pixel was painted in a frame, and red means 4x or more. Common causes are a window background plus layout backgrounds plus card backgrounds all being opaque. It says nothing about timing or software fallback.

questions.question: With hardware acceleration, what does the UI thread actually produce when a view's `onDraw()` runs?
options: Shader code that is compiled on the main thread
A bitmap of the view that is uploaded to the GPU each frame
A list of drawing commands recorded into the view's RenderNode, later replayed by the RenderThread
Pixels written directly into the window's buffer
questions.explanation: The hardware `Canvas` passed to `onDraw()` records operations into a display list on the view's RenderNode. The RenderThread then syncs the tree and turns those operations into GPU commands. The UI thread does not rasterize pixels itself.

questions.question: Why is animating `translationX` or `alpha` on a View cheaper than animating a custom property that you draw in `onDraw()`?
options: They trigger `requestLayout()` only once at the start
They are applied as RenderNode properties, so the display list does not need to be recorded again
Property changes skip the GPU completely
They run on a background thread instead of the UI thread
questions.explanation: Transform and alpha changes update the RenderNode's properties, and the existing display list is reused, so `onDraw()` is not called each frame. A custom property drawn in `onDraw()` needs `invalidate()` and re-recording every frame. The GPU still composes the result either way.

questions.question: Which of these commonly cause child views to be measured more than once per layout pass? Select all that apply.
options: A `LinearLayout` whose children use `layout_weight`
Changing a view's `alpha`
A `RelativeLayout`, which measures its children in two passes
Giving a view a fixed dp width and height
questions.explanation: Weighted LinearLayouts measure children once to find leftover space and again to distribute it, and RelativeLayout resolves horizontal and vertical rules in separate passes. Nested inside each other this grows quickly. Fixed sizes make measurement trivial, and alpha does not involve measurement at all.

questions.question: Some animations, such as the Material ripple, can keep running on the RenderThread even while the UI thread is briefly busy.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Ripples and other RenderNode-based animations are driven by the RenderThread, so they keep animating smoothly during a short UI-thread stall. Anything that needs new layout or a new display list still waits for the UI thread.

questions.question: A trace of the first frame of an image grid shows the UI thread finishing quickly, but the RenderThread spends a long time in slices about uploading bitmaps. What is the best fix?
options: Call `invalidate()` on each image view after binding
Decode images at the size they are displayed so less pixel data has to be uploaded to the GPU
Move `onBindViewHolder` to a background thread
Turn off hardware acceleration for the RecyclerView
questions.explanation: Software bitmaps must be uploaded to GPU textures the first time they are drawn, and the cost scales with pixel count. Oversized decodes make this slow, so downsampling helps the most. Disabling hardware acceleration makes everything slower, and binding is not the bottleneck here.

questions.question: You set `LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE` on a complex view while fading it in. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: If the view's content changes during the animation, the layer must be redrawn each time, losing the benefit
The layer moves the view's `onDraw()` onto the RenderThread
The view is rendered once into an offscreen texture, so alpha changes only recompose that texture
You should remove the layer when the animation ends, because it costs GPU memory
The layer permanently removes overdraw inside the view
questions.explanation: A hardware layer caches the view's rendering in a texture, so transform and alpha animations are cheap, but it costs memory and must be re-rendered whenever the content invalidates. `onDraw()` still runs on the UI thread, and overdraw inside the view still happens when the layer is rendered.

questions.question: A custom view calls `requestLayout()` at the end of every `onDraw()`. What happens?
options: Nothing, because requests made during draw are ignored
Only the view itself is measured again, at no extra cost
The app crashes with an exception about layout during draw
A new measure, layout and draw traversal is scheduled every frame, so the UI thread never goes idle
questions.explanation: `requestLayout()` marks the view and its ancestors dirty and schedules another traversal, which draws again and requests again, so the loop never ends. The result is constant CPU use and jank, not a crash, and the request is not limited to the single view.
